newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian leaders mark 43rd independence birthday.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian leaders mark 43rd independence birthday.

text.p: Cambodian leaders marked the nation's 43rd anniversary of independence from French colonial rule on Saturday, capping a week that saw the most significant strides towards true peace in more than two decades.
Parliament chief Chea Sim, standing in for head of state King Norodom Sihanouk, led a wreath-laying ceremony at Phnom Penh's imposing Independence Monument.
He was flanked by co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who were both wearing military uniforms of white tunics and black trousers with red stripes.
Ministers, military chiefs and diplomats followed the trio up a stairway of the monument as hundreds of schoolchildren looked on. The three released doves as balloons floated into the sky.

The ceremony came as Cambodia for the first time in decades appears close to achieving national peace. The nation has had a bloody history since Sihanouk won independence on November 9, 1953, ending 90 years of French colonial rule.

Thousands of Maoist Khmer Rouge rebels have agreed to join the government in recent weeks, eroding the military might of the once-feared movement that led a disastrous experiment in radical agrarian reform in the late 1970s.
The brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot left more than one million Cambodians dead from murder, malnutrition, disease and overwork.

The country had earlier been dragged into the Vietnam conflict after Sihanouk's overthrow in 1970. Communist Vietnamese forces, ironically, toppled the Khmer Rouge regime of their former ally Pol Pot in January 1979.

Civil war savaged the country until the main warring factions, including the Khmer Rouge, signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact in 1991. Elections in 1993 led to formation of a coalition headed by the parties of former battleffield foes, Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
The Khmer Rouge reneged on the pact and fought the government. But the movement has been unravelling since August, when former top cadre Ieng Sary split from Pol Pot and his hardliners.
His forces formally joined the government this week, following thousands of other guerrillas in the northwest and southwest of the country.
Hun Sen predicted earlier this week that the remainder of the hardline Khmer Rouge forces, estimated at up to 2,000, would be wiped out by mid-1997.
